projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Michael Salak was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Michael, M-I-C-H-A-E-L.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: S-A-L-A-K.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: S-A-L --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: A-K.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What was your birthday?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: One -- January 25, 1926.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What's your address?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: 312 Penn Avenue, Lyndora.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Penn with two Ns?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Penn with two Ns.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: 312 Penn Avenue, where?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: [Address deleted]

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What's your ZIP code?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: [zip code deleted]

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Your phone number?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: [Phone number deleted]

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you have Internet?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: You don't have Internet. What was your place of birth?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Right in the same house I live in. [Address deleted].

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What was the branch of service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Army.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Army.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Got out of the Army. Then I went into the armored division.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Armored division?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Serial number?

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: All right. Date of enlistment?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I was drafted in May of 1944. The date, I don't remember. And I was discharged in May of 1947.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What's your age?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Seventy-six.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What war were you in?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: World War II. Locations of military or civilian service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Where I was in service?

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Is that what -- okay. I went to Camp Blanding, Florida, for basic training.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: How do you spell that?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Blanding, B-L-A-N-D-I-N-G. Florida.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you say Camp Blanding?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Camp Blanding. Yeah. And I was there till November of 1945. And they shipped me from this camp for a week, this camp for a week. Then I went over to Texas. I never went overseas.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: You never went overseas?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I never went overseas.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So it was just like training and stuff?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, when I was in Florida, after I got in and had some training, I started to train a little bit. Then I started to drive a truck [inaudible], taking stuff to people that were out -- like out in the field. Food, ammunition and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Here's a release form. When you spell your name, do you put A-E, or is it E-A?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No. M-I-C-H-A-E-L.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: A-E-L.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: A-E-L.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: And we need your signature right there.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Uh-oh.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: It's just a release form.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I know that. I know.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I was drafted 19 -- in May of 1944.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: At that time, where were you living?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: At the same place.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: The same place?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Why did you pick -- did you pick your service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I tried to, but when you get drafted, they take you down to Pittsburgh, and then they -- they have four or five people there. I wanted the Navy. They stamped "Army."

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you recall any of your days in the service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, first days was rough. We left Pittsburgh -- I left Butler 6:00 in the evening. And we left Pittsburgh in the wee hours of the morning. We got in Cumberland And we were competing down there. We were up all night, all day and then the KP. It was a rough, rough first week. They put you to the test. And we were there for a couple days anyway at Camp Blanding, Florida in basic training. I remember one sergeant, Sergeant Chamber. He was a nice fellow. I mean, he was strict. That's fair. That's your nature.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Mm-hmm. It's like a football coach.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: If you're not in training, you [inaudible]. Let's say you're in the Army. They want you to abide by their rules. If you didn't, why, you got KP or glued to a tree or whatever. So you abide by their rules.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So what did it feel like? It was just like -- like a realization that --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: At first, you know, you're away from home, and you don't know what to expect, and you're kind of scared, actually, scared that you do right, you don't goof up. You're on what they call [inaudible]. Keep your nose clean.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Mm-hmm. So how was boot camp and the training? That was rough?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: That was rough.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Was it --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: You get up in the morning, I forget what time it was, but it was early. You went out and sweep the area. About an hour and a half later, you came in, went for breakfast for a week, and then you went out to a field, and you marched. You didn't skip right through it; you marched. Machine gun on your shoulder or a rifle and your backpack and whatnot. You walked. You marched. Maybe 5, 10 mile a day, and some of them are [inaudible] coming back. If you ate out in the field, you had a mess kit. They brought the feed to you. If it was raining, why, you was eating. You was eating from a swamp more or less. It was rough.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors and your --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Sergeant Chambers. I remember just the one. And Sergeant Nevins.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Were they, like, really cruel or --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No, no. They weren't cruel. They just wanted you to abide by the rules. Like I say, if you didn't abide by them, you -- you know, just like in school. If you don't abide by the rules, you get reprimanded.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: How did you get through boot camp?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I got through good, real, real good because I -- I was -- I was young, and I didn't weigh that much, maybe 148 pounds. I took it good. I was active before I went in, so I didn't get as -- I mean, you got tired, believe me. But I got through it okay.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So you didn't even -- so you didn't get to go overseas?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So what was your, like, job or assignment instead of going over? What did you do exactly?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, like I say, I stayed in the -- Florida. I trained some kids for a while there. Then when they got -- say a new crew would come in. I would help them, get them critiqued, more or less, like marching and stuff. You get a lot of guys who come in the Army. They didn't know their left from their right. You've got to left, right, left, right. And you've got to more or less, in small groups, teach them. Then when they got, say, a week or so, then they went on, you know, out, try to see if they could drive a truck -- whatever.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, the first time I was ever in a hurricane was in Florida. I remember that. I didn't get -- nobody got hurt, but it was -- when you get in a hurricane for the first time, you don't know what to expect. Otherwise, [inaudible] stateside, I don't remember nothing. Well, like when you took basic training, you had to crawl on the ground. They had a machine gun.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Barbed wire?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: It weren't barbed wire. You couldn't get up. They had a machine gun firing over your head. If you got up, you were dead. They told you that. And you got to crawl from one spot to the other -- like, say, the machine guns were behind here; you've got to crawl from here, maybe twice as far as this. And the machine guns were firing live ammunition. Done at night and during the day. At night, they had tracers. You could see them tracers going over your head.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: I would be scared.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah. I'd be scared.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Then like down in Texas, I was still in fatigues. You've got rattlesnakes. Now, we had rattlesnakes in Florida, too. I learned a lot. I mean, I think it taught you discipline. Back in '44, they didn't have no -- what you say? Dope and stuff like that like they have today.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: And money was tight. At first -- the beginning of World War II, have to say you got paid $21 a day once a month. And later, I got $37 a day once a month. You have to buy [inaudible] if you smoke. Toiletry. If you wanted to go to town, you had a few bucks for a few beers and whatever. Like I say, money was scarce. Well, of course you got three meals a day and a roof over your head.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No. Just good conduct and victory medal. And the tank, Second Armored Division, the French gave what they called a Croix de guerre. It was a [inaudible] anybody from the armored division got one. It's a French citation because of the [inaudible] in Europe in World War II. Like I say, there's one guy that I knew at basic training who got killed and another guy lost his leg from Butler. And then when you got in boot camp, there was people from all over the country: Kentucky, Tennessee, Maine, Massachusetts, New York. [inaudible]. You got to know a lot of people.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: In your rank of being, like, a sergeant --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: -- how high is that up on the --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, you've got private, private first class, corporal. That's three stripes.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Like, how much higher can you go?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, master sergeant or first sergeant. You've got three [inaudible] for each of them and three underneath [inaudible]. The master sergeant -- the first sergeant has got the star in the middle. The first sergeant has a -- just the three underneath.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you do any, like, battle planning at all?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: No battle planning?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes. When you -- when you're in basic training, they have places where you sit in the back, and they have like hedgerows up front. See, the enemy is over there. They sort of pop up targets [inaudible]. And you have like that machine gun, you keep on strafing; just went one side to the other. And then you -- a regular rifleman fired at what he saw. The machine gunner would try to keep their heads down, like you do -- well, you hide behind something. That machine gun, it just strafes across everything. They teach you to do that.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: That sounds cool.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: See, either machine gunner, Browning automatic rifleman or a rifleman. There's three categories. Or a mortarman, too.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Is that of the, like, Army? Just the Army?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Are there any, like, jump trooper people, like paratroopers or --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I wasn't in then when they -- they had them. They trained in Fort Benning, Georgia at the time, all paratroopers.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: How'd you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, wrote letters. Back then, hardly anybody had telephones actually. A telephone was an expensive item. Now they have all kinds of them, cell phones and whatnot. Just wrote letters.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: They have cell phones. Everyone has a cell phone in the --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. I don't care for them.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: I don't have one either.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: You get these people going down the road on the telephone. Their mind is on the telephone --

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: And not driving.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, it wasn't bad. They gave you -- just like in a hospital. They gave you food that was high in calories and everything else. But it's not like home cooking, you know. Everything is -- it was good. A lot of times, you didn't get enough.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah. That's like that with school food, too. They don't give you enough.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Right. I was going to say in school, they don't give you enough, and it's not like home cooking.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Nothing is. Did you have plenty of supplies when you went?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. They made sure that everybody had supplies, you know. Like I said, I drove a truck, and I would -- you know, the kids were out in the fields training. And I would take them -- let's see. Ammunition, shells or mortars or whatever. And I would deliver the food, too.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you feel pressure or stress during this time?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Not really. No. I -- let me see. I went in to do the job the best I knew how.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: How were your -- like, your feelings after you were drafted? How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I was scared. I was worried because you didn't know what was going to happen. Get sent overseas. Like I say, there's lots and lots of people got killed. Like you probably know a lot of people -- don't remember them, but people who got killed in World War II. I mean, your relatives probably. You were scared. Anybody that wasn't, something's funny.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Because like I say, if you're going to go over -- in fact, I'm glad I didn't go over. But I went -- I went where they sent me. Wasn't a heck of a lot I could have done about it. You feel like you're on a ship, going over. Submarine, torpedo or whatever. How many people got torpedoed. Or the Japanese with their kamikaze. You don't know what to expect. Like today, Paris.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That's bad, too. How'd you entertain yourself?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, they had what they called ?bank hitter?, base centers. You could go down there, and they had, like, ping pong and pool. They would bring you the -- some acts or a little orchestra sometimes, every once a month or whatever. They would bring in girls. You could dance, meet some girls.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: That sounds cool.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. They had like a PX. It would be like a restaurant. You could get something to eat, something to drink, whatever. It was like a regular PX. They sold everything. Milk, shirts.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Was this, like, on camp? Was this --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Every so far, they would have a PX.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: When on leave, what did you do? What did you do on leave?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I went to Jacksonville. That was in Florida. I went to Ocala. I went to Orlando -- not Orlando, but Gainesville. Then like in Texas -- well, in Texas I went to Austin, Texas. Waco. A few other places there. Just see the country. Believe it or not, I'm going to tell you a story. When I was in Texas, they sent us to ?Jonestown/Galveston?. For one week, we went on vacation. We just went there on the coast. We did what we wanted to. It was free. Wasn't much money. Went down in trucks [inaudible] out in the yard.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Probably couldn't wait to get down there.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. And then back again. It was a good week.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Probably seemed like a long ride going back.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Then I got troop trained from -- in Virginia. We went for troop training [inaudible] steam engine back then. We had the windows open, was black smoke coming in from Virginia down to Texas. It was hot.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you recall any particularly, like, humorous events, humorous or unusual?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No. Not really.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What were, like, some of the pranks you guys would pull on each other [inaudible]?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you a little story. When I was in boot camp, this guy, he was from Kentucky. You heard of people that didn't wear his shoes. He was one of them, and he didn't take a shower. So when you got hot in the field, hot sweat, you don't take a shower, you don't wash your clothes, and everything stinks. He told the sergeant. He says, "You know what they do in the Army?" He says, "You grab him" -- there was six in a hut. Had double bunks. And I had to sleep above this guy. So the sergeant says, "You know what you do in the Army?" He says, "All five of you guys grab him and take him in the shower. You can scrub him down." That's right. We had to do that to teach him to take a shower. He never had shoes till he got in the Army. He couldn't -- some who were drafted had to go to school to learn to read and write.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: In the Army? When they were in it?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. They'd be -- yeah. They had school to teach them to read and write.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: So for some people, the Army was, like, real beneficial?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Anybody. I mean, to tell you the truth, they should draft them at least a year. Discipline. A lot of -- all the kids aren't bad. But some of these kids, they need to be disciplined.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Responsibility and --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Like you probably know people who are nice [inaudible] what they call a jack-off, you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Talk to you like -- you guys are old enough to [inaudible]. They think they're it. Showoffs.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: You guys -- you've got them everywhere.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you have any photographs?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: You know what? I never was into that. You have guys that take them. I never [inaudible].

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What did you think of officers and fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, some officers were -- they were keen, what they called 90-day wonders. Sent them to school for 90 days, make them a second lieutenant. They [inaudible]. Just like a steel mill do the same thing. These guys come out of college, and the book tells you you do this, you do that. But to do the actual work, it's different. You take like in a melt shop [inaudible] the steel. These guys come out of college, say cook them for, say, eight hours. These guys went up through the ranks. They don't go by the book. Just like in the Army. Same thing. Guys do what they're taught sometimes.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you, like, keep a personal diary at all?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Never. No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We all got paid the day before you're supposed to [inaudible], they take you in and examine you, make sure you're all right. Then the next day, they give you your money for -- to get home on. You can get home any way you wanted to: a plane, bus, hitchhike or what. They allotted you so much money to travel.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Where were you when your service ended?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: In Campbell, Texas.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Texas?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Texas.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: What did you do in the days and weeks afterwards?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I did nothing. They had what they call a 52-20. You got $3 a week -- a month for -- well, $20 a week for 52 weeks. I did that for [inaudible].

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you go to school afterwards? Did you go back to school or --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Was it supported by the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I could have went back on the GI Bill, if I wanted to. I started, but then it was too rough. I was working and had to go to school in Pittsburgh. It was too many hours.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Not enough time?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Not enough time. I'd get out of work, have to go to Pittsburgh in the evening. I had to work two shifts, 3 to 11. When I was working 3 to 11, I could go in the morning. When I was working daylight, I could go in the evening. It was too rough.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I did, but I didn't keep contact.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: You didn't keep in contact?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No. I did for a while. Then you get married and whatever and [inaudible] with a baby.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Were you married before --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: -- you went into the service?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you get married afterwards?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. I got married -- they discharged me in '47. I got married in April in 1953.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you join any, like, veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: American Legion.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: American Legion.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I was chaplain for a while. We're building a Post 778 in Lyndora. We're building a new post, up past the -- do you know where the old Lyndora school used to be?

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: I'm not from around here.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, you're not from around here? Oh. We bought 21 acres. [inaudible] We bought a tank, and we put it in front of our lot, this camouflage paint. It's in front of our lot and our building. Now ready to put up our new home as soon as the weather breaks.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah. This weather is horrible.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yes. So we can't do nothing. We went and got all of the ironwork, and everything is there, but the weather's been bad.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Where are you from?

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: I'm from PA. Paxton Do you know where Newcastle is?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, you come from different schools.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: No. We go to the same school. Just different areas. We go to Mount [inaudible]

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, okay. I know where -- Mohawk Okay. I know where -- Mohawk Country Club. It's on 224.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Chris Fowler works there. He's [inaudible]. He works for the country club. Did your experience change your thinking about the military or wars?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Sometimes I wished I'd have stayed and retired from the military because, you know, you figure, well -- at the time, you wanted to get out. The war was over in '45 in August or September, something like that. And I had another -- I was in there for another year and a half. You were happy to get out. Later on, I wished I'd stayed and retired after 20 years. Then you could have got an easy job on the outside and draw a pension. Easy jobs.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: And the health benefits.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Well, like the VA here, the veterans. They can only do so much. Where'd you come in?

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Auditorium.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, okay. Down at the end of this hall is where people come in with the register to see a doctor. Your prescriptions are $7. The services connected with it are free. If you have high blood pressure or something, they charge you $7. It used to be 2. In February, it went up to 7.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Big jump.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. But they're still cheap. But like I say, my one prescription would be $68. Now, it's only $2. Now, it's only 7. On the outside, it was $68.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: You save a lot of money up here.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, yeah. [inaudible] being in the service helped. They treat you -- they come up. They wanted every veteran to come up and register because they're closing some of these places down. Get the veterans in to show them that these [inaudible]. I don't know how many people every day. Like I say, down the end of the hall is where they call primary care. There's a [inaudible] you've got to register, get your name in the computer. Once your name is in the computer, if something happened, you know, they can treat you here. All you've got to do is give the last four numbers of your social security number, and you've got all your history. The records are here.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No, no. No. I haven't been. In peacetime over at the second armory, I never got a letter, but the ones that were in the war, they probably had one. I probably could go, but I wouldn't know anybody. Unless there were some of the guys that [inaudible]. Mostly for guys who went overseas have one.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did your service and experiences affect your life at all?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: It didn't affect it much at all?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Like I say, discipline is what they taught you. You've got to carry on through life. You can't just go out -- like today, [inaudible] kids are misbehaving and all that stuff --

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: -- in school. Dope. It's just bad.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Bad, bad, bad.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Is there anything you'd like to add that we haven't covered at all? Anything you'd like to talk about?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No. Just I'm happy that you come, and try to give you my experience. Like I say, the other guys probably have more to say than I. They were overseas. I was just stateside. I went where they sent me. That was it. Like I say, there was one fellow from here got killed. Went to basic training with me. He went overseas. One guy got his leg shot off. I was a lucky man, more or less.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah. I'd like stay overseas. How do you feel about the draft, about the draft coming up --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I think that -- like I told you before, I think when you become 18, you should -- you have to register. And they should put you in the army for one year. Give you basic training, a little bit -- critique you on weapons and stuff like that and what's going on and what could happen. They taught them kids how to shoot the Vietnamese, even women. Like we've already seen in Paris. They're not like -- I was never in Vietnam. So it's a great experience.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Do you think in this, like, draft coming up, do you think women should be drafted as well as men?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I think women should stay at home. They don't have the strength to be. Not like state police or whatever. I think they should be -- You ever see how some small some of these women are? I mean --

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: There's only a select few that could, that --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. But I'm not one to say they can't. Like in a steel mill, too. They can't do a man's job. Some in the office, but to go out and do manual labor in the steel mill? Well, today, maybe yes. When I started, everything was by hand.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: And then it's all automatic now.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Robots and computers.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Still you have to know a little bit about [inaudible] to know how to coil steel. Before, you had to break it down, what they call break it down, you get it straight so you can put it up there in a set of pincers that are turning and take it through. Now it's everything automatic.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Too bad there aren't any, like, steel mills left.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, Pittsburgh was great. It was steel capital of the world.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Well, we'd just like to thank you for sharing your reflections with us.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Well, I'm glad -- I have to do this. There's supposed to be a couple other buddies of mine that were supposed to be here, and they never showed up. They signed up, but they never showed up.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: No-shows.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I gave you what I thought, you know -- being stateside, you probably would have got more out of them other guys of the, you know, overseas and stuff.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Did they go overseas?

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Yeah. Them guys were overseas. One guy was a lieutenant colonel.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Is that high up? Is that --

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: That's high.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: That's -- lieutenant colonel. When you become a -- it's a silver leaf. Next one is a colonel. It's an eagle. Then you go up to be lieutenant. You've got lieutenant, first lieutenant, captain, major, lieutenant colonel, colonel and -- you know. Brigadier, general, major general, lieutenant general and general. Okay. So I'm glad I gave you what I thought. That was the best I know, not being overseas. Yeah. I thought the way they were going to work was I would talk a while to whoever -- I was going to be the first one because I know the other guys were overseas. See, I wasn't. I was going to make my talk a little short because, you know, they would give you more experience because they were overseas. I would give you experience stateside. Then they would give the experience wherever they were, Germany or Italy or France. Africa. They start out in Africa. I had one cousin that was killed in Italy. At Anzio, Anzio beachhead. If you ever saw this one picture in Time magazine a few years ago. It's been two or three years, but here about two years ago, they had this one guy. He was from Lyndora. They were dragging him in Normandy. They dragged him in from the water onto the beach because he got hit. They dragged him in to the beach. He just died here a couple years ago. He would be 80, 81 years old. Time -- well, a few magazines. I have them at home. I wished I'd have brought them. We're wrapped up. I'm just giving -- okay. Okay, fellows.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Thanks.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: No problem.

sp.speaker: Jonathan Dale
sp.p: Yeah. Thanks a lot.

sp.speaker: Michael Salak
sp.p: I'm glad I could help you out. (Conclusion of interview.)
